Typhoid Fever — A Public Health Reference Guide
Health awareness chatbot knowledge base entry
Overview
Typhoid fever is a serious illness caused by bacteria called Salmonella Typhi. It spreads mainly through food and water that have been contaminated with the germ, usually through unsafe handling of human waste. The bacteria enter the body through the mouth, travel through the gut, and then spread into the bloodstream, causing fever and illness throughout the body.
Typhoid is common in areas with unsafe drinking water and poor sanitation, and it remains a public health concern in many parts of India, including Odisha. It can affect people of any age, but children and young adults are frequently affected. With timely medical care, most people recover fully. Without proper treatment, typhoid can become severe and, in rare cases, life-threatening.
Common Symptoms
Typhoid usually develops slowly, with symptoms appearing about one to three weeks after exposure to the bacteria. Common signs include:
Fever that starts low and gradually rises over several days, often becoming very high
Persistent headache
Weakness, fatigue, and body aches
Loss of appetite
Stomach pain or discomfort
Constipation or, in some people, loose stools
Nausea
In some cases, a rash of small flat, rose-coloured spots on the chest or abdomen
Symptoms often build up gradually rather than appearing suddenly, and the fever tends to stay high and does not go away with rest alone. If untreated, symptoms can become more severe over the following weeks.
Causes
Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, which lives only in humans. A person becomes infected mainly by:
Drinking water that has been contaminated with human waste
Eating food prepared or washed with contaminated water
Eating food handled by a person carrying the bacteria who did not wash their hands properly
Eating raw fruits or vegetables that were washed in unsafe water
Some people who recover from typhoid can continue to carry the bacteria in their body for a long time without feeling sick themselves, and can still spread it to others through poor hand hygiene. This is why safe water, sanitation, and hygiene practices are so important in preventing typhoid, both for the sick person and for the wider community.
When to See a Doctor — Red-Flag Warning Signs
Typhoid needs proper medical diagnosis and treatment. Do not try to manage it with home remedies alone. See a doctor or health worker promptly if a person has:
Fever that continues for more than two to three days, especially if it keeps rising
High fever that does not improve with rest and fluids
Severe or worsening stomach pain
Ongoing vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down
Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools
Severe weakness, confusion, difficulty staying awake, or unusual drowsiness
Signs of dehydration, such as very little urine, dry mouth, or sunken eyes
Fast or difficult breathing
Fever in a young child, elderly person, pregnant woman, or anyone with an existing serious illness
These signs may point to a severe infection or a complication and need urgent medical attention. Suspected typhoid should always be confirmed and treated by a qualified doctor, since correct treatment matters for full recovery and for preventing the person from spreading the infection to others.
Home Care and Prevention
If a doctor has diagnosed typhoid and is guiding treatment, simple supportive care at home can help the person feel better and recover:
Get plenty of rest
Drink plenty of clean, safe fluids to prevent dehydration, especially if there is fever or loose stools
Eat light, easily digestible food as appetite allows
Follow the doctor's advice fully and complete the full course of any treatment given, even if the person starts to feel better
Keep the sick person's utensils, clothing, and bedding separate, and wash them properly
Always wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before preparing or eating food, especially while someone in the household is unwell
Typhoid can largely be prevented by protecting water and food from contamination. Households and communities can reduce risk by:
Drinking only safe water — boiled, filtered, or from a protected, tested source
Storing drinking water in a clean, covered container
Washing hands with soap before eating, before cooking, and after using the toilet
Washing fruits and vegetables with safe water before eating
Eating freshly cooked, hot food, and avoiding food from unhygienic surroundings
Using a proper toilet and avoiding open defecation
Asking a health worker about the typhoid vaccine, which is available in some immunization programmes for children and can offer added protection
Odisha-Specific Notes
In many rural parts of Odisha, drinking water still comes from tube wells, dug wells, or other sources that are not always tested or protected from contamination, and a large share of households do not treat their water before drinking it. Studies from rural Odisha have also found that open defecation continues in some communities, which increases the risk of water and food contamination and the spread of typhoid and similar illnesses. There have also been local outbreaks reported in the state linked to contaminated water sources, underlining why safe water practices matter.
Families in rural Odisha can protect themselves by always boiling or properly filtering drinking water, keeping water storage containers covered and clean, using a toilet instead of open defecation, and washing hands with soap at key times such as before meals and after using the toilet. Government programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission (for safe piped water to rural households) and Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen (for sanitation and ending open defecation) support these efforts in Odisha. The National Health Mission, Odisha, along with ASHA and Anganwadi workers, also promotes hygiene education and can guide families on safe water and food practices and where to seek care.
Anyone in Odisha with an unexplained continuing fever, especially during the monsoon or summer months when water contamination risk is higher, should visit the nearest sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital rather than waiting for symptoms to worsen.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), and the National Health Mission, Odisha. It reflects widely accepted, general awareness-level information and does not cite specific studies or figures from any single publication.
Sources consulted: World Health Organization (who.int); National Health Mission, India (nhm.gov.in); National Health Mission, Odisha (nhmodisha.gov.in); Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen, Government of India.
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
